To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Brugada syndrome can be diagnosed by an abnormal ECG, that the disease can be genetically heterogeneous, that the ECG can be influenced by many external factors, that the disease is not always present, that it is not always symptomatic, and that the diagnosis of asymptomatic patients is still a challenge.
Brugada Syndrome is a disease caused by genetic mutations that can be diagnosed by an abnormal ECG, and that it has an excellent prognosis when treated with an implantable cardioverter defibrillator.
Brugada Ecg is a genetic disease, that the ECG is variable and that asymptomatic individuals with the disease exist.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification and characterization of genetic mutations that cause Brugada syndrome and the development and validation of diagnostic tools to identify the individuals who will develop sudden death.
the identification of the molecular basis of the Brugada syndrome and the development of diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.
the clinical diagnosis, pathogenesis, genetics, and management of Brugada and other inherited arrhythmia syndromes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Brugada Syndrome is a disease of the cardiac sodium channel that may be inherited in an autosomal dominant or recessive fashion.
the Brugada Ecg is the most important diagnostic tool for Brugada syndrome but it has to be interpreted in the context of the clinical presentation of the patient and the genetic status.
Brugada is an important disease, with a high risk for sudden death and a very heterogeneous genetic background.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the clinical diagnosis of Brugad syndrome remains the ECG.
Brugada Syndrome is a disease of the cardiac sodium channel, which is genetically heterogeneous.
the Brugada EKG is the most important clue to the diagnosis of Brugad syndrome and the most important risk factor for the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diagnosis of Brugad syndrome should only be made when there is a strong suspicion based on the history of syncope or sudden death in the family.
the ECG remains the key for diagnosis and that the diagnosis of Brugad syndrome should be made with the patient in a state of normal heart rate and rhythm.
the Brugada syndrome has become a model for the study of the genetic basis of cardiac arrhythmias.
